FAST

SYDNEY, Oct 12 : Asian share markets got off to a cautious start on Monday as earnings season loomed as a challenge to sky-high tech valuations, while oil was choppy after strikes on shipping and airports in the Gulf. There was considerable confusion about President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, which neither side had confirmed. Trump's proposal for Russia to increase its exports of diesel was also under fire from Republican and Democratic senators as potentially illegal. Brent futures started higher but soon slipped 1.1 per cent to $103.50 a barrel, away from the recent top of $109.97, while US crude futures lost 1.2 per cent to $90.73 a barrel.

South Korean stocks fell 1.1 per cent, while MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan was little changed. On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures edged up 0.2 per cent, while Nasdaq futures firmed 0.5 per cent. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.4 per cent, while DAX futures gained 0.4 per cent and FTSE futures added 0.3 per cent. Trade was thin with Japan markets shut and the US on a partial holiday ahead of the earnings season with major US banks kicking off on Tuesday. S&P 500 earnings are expected to have jumped by more than 30 per cent in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES, though the bulk of that comes from the tech sector. My Bui, an economist at AMP, noted all the gains in the S&P 500 since mid-September had been in tech, while investors were demanding higher yields to fund the massive borrowing for AI. The US investment-grade credit default swap index, which tracks the cost of insurance against default, had also risen sharply to its highest level since the Iran war began. "Overall, wider spreads suggest investors are questioning whether AI revenues can keep pace with rising borrowing costs," added Bui. "Corporate bond issuance to fund AI capex, combined with wider high-yield spreads, will raise refinancing costs as the current wave of debt matures over the next few years." US CPI TO HEAT UP, BUT CORE COOLER The flood of corporate debt has added to pressure in sovereign markets, driving Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week and lifting the discount applied to company earnings. The market faces fresh challenges this week from US data on consumer and producer prices and retail sales. Rising energy costs are expected to lift CPI by a hefty 0.6 per cent to an annual 3.7 per cent, though the core is seen cooler at 0.2 per cent and 2.5 per cent. "Oil prices remain higher than we had assumed as shipping costs have soared, and product prices are even higher," said Bruce Kasman, head of global economics at JPMorgan. "The signals on inflation point to a sharp rebound in headline inflation that will squeeze purchasing power and a firming in core inflation that will keep central banks focused on near-term hikes." Markets imply only an 18 per cent chance of a rate rise from the Federal Reserve this month, but an 85 per cent chance of a hike in December. Investors are also wagering on hikes in the EU, Japan and UK before year end. In currency markets, the euro remained on the defensive at $1.1201 having fallen for five weeks straight amid concerns about government deficits in Europe. The dollar index held near 17-month highs at 102.25, but has stalled on the yen at 158.15 as the threat of Japanese intervention deters speculators for now. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold rose 0.3 per cent to $4,206 an ounce, having managed to bounce more than 1 per cent last week.

Source: Reuters

RIYADH: One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday (Oct 11), Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. Coalition forces also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted.  Emergency alerts were also issued in Abha, in the south, early on Monday but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said.

The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in. The airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said the group had struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco. The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment. The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way."

Related:

Saudi Arabia says three killed at airport as Yemen war expands

Singapore condemns Houthi attacks on civilian aviation infrastructure in Saudi Arabia

An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8.30pm (1.30am, Monday, Singapore time) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures at Dammam airport, the kingdom's third-largest. The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said. Britain's embassy in Saudi Arabia in a post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina. US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom. "WORSE IS YET TO COME," HOUTHIS WARN Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. In a post on Telegram, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Related:

Türkiye sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say

ENERGY CONFERENCE STILL GOING AHEAD A five-day conference of international energy organisation WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km from the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said. A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ministers attended. Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link. German officials were trying to organise a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday but the ministry said it appeared likely her flight would be unable to take off. Separately, Saudi authorities announced that in-person classes at schools in Riyadh would be shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday. Sunday's attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh's airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday's attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign nationals, Saudi authorities said.

Source: Reuters/rk

The Trump administration has reversed a decision that requested developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic not to share new AI models with Britain's AI Security Institute before release, the newspaper said.

FAST

LONDON: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia interfered in the 2016 Brexit vote, as he warned voters in France and Germany about Moscow-backed efforts to influence their politics. Burnham, who took over as Britain's leader in July and said last month that Britain could consider rejoining the European Union in the future, is the first British prime minister to say openly there was evidence of Russian interference in the referendum a decade ago. "I asked the question coming to Downing Street, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I've had the clear answer that yes, there was," Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday (Oct 11). Burnham did not spell out how he believed that Russia interfered in the referendum and gave no details on what evidence this statement was based.

Burnham's comments mark a departure from those of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU, and said in 2020 there was no evidence of Russian interference in the referendum. Britons voted 52 per cent to 48 per cent to leave the EU in 2016, plunging the country into its biggest political crisis since World War II. Burnham said voters in European democracies needed to be better informed about efforts to disrupt their politics. "I mean, these things are important now to put clearly on the record, and I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said. Britain's government failed to establish whether Russia meddled in the 2016 referendum on membership of the EU, according to a report by parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee in 2020. The report also found that Russia had sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, in which voters rejected independence. Burnham last month said he could campaign to take Britain back into the EU at the next general election, reopening the country’s divisive debate on its relationship with the continent.

Source: Reuters/fs

FAST

LIVERPOOL, Oct 11 : Manchester City have spent the last two weeks surrounded by a lot of noise. On Sunday at Anfield, City boss Enzo Maresca told his players the best way to drown it out was by making even more of their own. City did just that with a defiant 3-0 victory over Liverpool that preserved their perfect Premier League start for a three-point lead atop the table. In their first game since an independent commission found the club guilty of 114 breaches of the league's financial rules, City were met by deafening boos and angry chants but left Anfield with their own supporters providing the soundtrack. It was exactly the response Maresca had demanded from his players.

"We need to learn how to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, and the noise will be always there," Maresca said. "But at the same time, we need to try to make our noise, and that is win games, like we have done today, because at the end of the game, our fans, they were singing, so the noise was from us, not from Liverpool." The Italian knows the hostility is unlikely to disappear, with Sunday's reception at Anfield a sign of what awaits City on their travels as they await the outcome of their appeal against the financial-rule verdict. "I think (at) all the away games there's going to be noise," said Maresca, who wrapped his coaching staff in a huge hug at the final whistle before he and the players made a beeline for the away fans section to celebrate. "That's why I'm saying that we need to learn how to deal with noise, but at the same time we need to make our noise. Our noise is: who is singing at the end? This has to be our target in this moment." City's response on the pitch matched one of defiance off it. The club's chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana travelled with the team to Anfield, a show of unity ahead of one of the most daunting fixtures on the calendar even in less turbulent times. "We were all together," Maresca said. "I think for the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away, it's a good idea from the club to be all together, the togetherness that in this moment we need." The manager said the players had found the last fortnight difficult, but praised the way they had shut out the turmoil and concentrated on football. City struggled in the first half but took full control after Liverpool's Ryan Gravenberch was shown a red card in the 62nd minute, with Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki scoring. "It was not easy for the players after the last two weeks," he said. "I think they dealt with all the situation very well. "In this moment, all the organisation needs this kind of win like today," he added. "It's good for us coaching staff. It's good for the players. It's good for the fans. It's good for the organisation." City have denied all wrongdoing and have appealed the decision. As for what comes next in their legal battle, Maresca was just as direct. "I'm here to try to prepare for the games and win games," he said. "I've said many times: hopefully, I can speak about this situation when we win the appeal." For now, City's answer to the hostility: not to quieten the racket, but to drown it out with the sounds of victory.

Source: Reuters

Oct 11 : Real Betis playmaker Isco netted a goal in each half as his side breezed to a 5-2 home win over Osasuna on Sunday that lifts them to third place in LaLiga, five points behind leaders Barcelona and one ahead of Real Madrid.  Isco fired home from the penalty spot in the 10th minute to open the scoring, and Abde Ezzalzouli added a second before the break after Betis won the ball high up the pitch and countered quickly.  Betis looked to be set for a comfortable afternoon when Diego Llorente added a third three minutes after halftime, but two quick goals for the visitors from Ante Budimir and Raul Garcia reduced the deficit to 3-2 in the 56th minute. However, Isco eased their nerves again when he snapped up a loose ball in the box and rifled it home, and Jose Antonio Morante came off the bench in the 90th minute to make his LaLiga debut before scoring deep into stoppage time to leave Betis on 19 points after eight games.

Earlier on Sunday, Real Sociedad held off a spirited comeback from Deportivo La Coruna to emerge with a 3-2 win at home, while struggling Elche grabbed a much-needed point by holding visitors Celta Vigo to a scoreless draw.   In the evening's late kick-off, second-from-bottom Valencia came back from a goal down to grab a point in a 2-2 draw away to Racing Santander.  Dani Raba got the visitors off to a great start when he latched on to a long ball and kept his cool to cut inside two defenders and fire home in the second minute to give his side a 1-0 lead, but Yassir Zabiri levelled in the 32nd minute with a finish low into the bottom corner. Ivan Martin gave the home side the lead two minutes into the second half but 18-year-old substitute David Otorbi grabbed a point for Valencia with a well-taken finish in the 65th minute.   Valencia are 19th on five points after eight games, one ahead of bottom side Malaga and behind Levante on goal difference. Elche are one point above the drop zone and ahead of Valencia, while 16th-placed Osasuna were among a cluster of eight teams locked on eight points.

REGGIO EMILIA, Italy, Oct 11 : Lazio maintained their impressive start to the season with a 3-1 win over Monza on Sunday to move level on points with Serie A leaders Inter Milan, while Juventus rescued a 1-1 draw at high-flying Cagliari. Ten-man AS Roma held on to draw 0-0 at Como and AC Milan were pegged back in a 1-1 draw at Sassuolo. Inter moved to 16 points with Saturday's 3-0 win over Parma and Lazio joined them despite almost allowing 10-man Monza back in the game. Roma are two points behind in third, with Cagliari fourth on 13 points and Milan a further point back in fifth spot. Juventus and Como are on 11 points. Gennaro Gattuso's Lazio took a third-minute lead at the Stadio Olimpico when Nuno Tavares rifled an unstoppable shot into the roof of the net.

Midway through the first half, Lazio doubled their advantage with Gustav Isaksen finding the far bottom corner with a first-time shot from wide in the box. Monza's comeback chances then took a hammering when they had Lorenzo Lucchesi sent off 10 minutes before the break. Instead, Lazio appeared to switch off, and Monza pulled one back in the opening minute of the second half. Dany Mota flicked on a corner for Saba Goglichidze to head home, and for long periods the visitors had Lazio under the cosh. Mota was twice denied by Lazio keeper Christos Mandas before Lazio regrouped and finished off Monza's challenge two minutes from time through Andrea Pinamonti's strike from the edge of the six-yard box. "We can't afford to play like we did in the second half," Gattuso told DAZN. "We shouldn't be trying to manage the game. We need to keep doing things the right way." ROMA AND MILAN LOSE GROUND Roma were without injured keeper Mile Svilar, allowing Pierluigi Gollini to make his first league appearance since joining the club in January 2025. Gollini was in action early on, denying Nico Paz's attempted chip and at the other end Lorenzo Pellegrini's shot hit the upright in an evenly contested opening half. It was mostly one-way traffic, however, once Roma's Donyell Malen was sent off eight minutes after the break and Como piled on the pressure in search of a winner. Tasos Douvikas fired a shot into the side netting, and Gollini again saved from Paz as Roma hung on to earn a point in the first scoreless draw of the season in Serie A. Milan also lost ground on the leaders after surrendering a second-half advantage at Sassuolo, although they remain unbeaten this season. Sassuolo keeper Arijanet Muric made saves from Goncalo Ramos, Diego Moreira and Strahinja Pavlovic to keep the game goalless at the break. Milan introduced Luka Modric from the bench at the start of the second half, and the Croatian playmaker set up the opening goal in the 63rd minute with a pass into Adrien Rabiot, who scored from a tight angle. Sassuolo levelled five minutes later, Cas Odenthal firing past Mike Maignan through a crowded six-yard box following a corner kick. Cagliari, who had won four of their opening five matches, appeared on course for another victory after Daniel Maldini gave them a 20th-minute lead against Juventus. The visitors rescued a draw nine minutes from time when substitute Kerim Alajbegovic crossed to the back post for Randal Kolo Muani to score his first league goal of the season. Juventus manager Luciano Spalletti and his Cagliari counterpart Fabio Pisacane were both shown red cards following a verbal altercation after the final whistle.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday (Oct 11) in response to critical comments from US President Donald Trump that he will organise elections in Ukraine if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day ceasefire. "Please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organise elections," Zelenskyy told ABC's This Week. Trump on Saturday criticised Zelenskyy for attacking Russian oil refineries a day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed to deprive Moscow of revenues to fund its war in Ukraine. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump had told reporters at the White House.

Under terms of the deal as described by Trump on Friday, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, equal to about 2.25 million barrels of fuel. Trump is under pressure to bring down rising fuel prices ahead of November midterm elections that will determine whether his Republican Party will retain control of the US Congress for his final two years in office. LIVERPOOL, Oct 11 : Manchester City silenced a hostile Anfield crowd as second-half goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki secured a 3-0 victory over 10-man Liverpool on Sunday and maintained the Premier League leaders' perfect start to the season. City were playing for the first time since an independent commission found them guilty of 114 breaches of the league's financial rules, and were greeted by deafening boos and angry chants. But Enzo Maresca's side stood firm against Liverpool's early pressure and a fevered atmosphere before taking control after Ryan Gravenberch was sent off in the 62nd minute for a second booking following a foul on Doku. HAALAND SPARKS CITY ROUT

Haaland then struck three minutes later, smashing a left-footed shot past Alisson after Doku worked the ball into the box and his attempted shot was deflected into the path of the big Norwegian. Haaland made a beeline to celebrate with the travelling City fans including Oasis frontman Noel Gallagher. Doku doubled the lead in the 68th minute with a gorgeous long-range shot that curled into the far top corner. Cherki completed the rout - and sent scores of Liverpool fans heading to the exits - in the 78th minute when he let the ball roll through to Josko Gvardiol before turning into the box to meet his teammate's pass and slot the ball home. "It was a lovely moment that will stay with us a long time," Man City striker Haaland told Sky Sports. "It’s time to stay strong and stick together and do what you can do something about, stick together." Man City midfielder Elliot Anderson said City's unity had stood out. "We've shown real togetherness and fight. It's a tough place to come and it's challenging," he said. "We really stuck together out there, fought for each other and played well." The Liverpool fans left at the final whistle chanted "Going down! Going Down! Going Down!" in reference to City's potential relegation. The club have denied all wrongdoing, and have appealed the independent commission's verdict. CITY DELIVER DEFIANT RESPONSE A defiant Haaland and Maresca grinned and pumped their fists at the City fans, who delightedly waved inflatable bananas, a tradition dating from their time out of the top flight in the 1980s. "Very difficult circumstances and environment," Maresca said. "We need to learn how to deal with the noise because the noise will be with us for all the away games. "And (we need to) make our noise, and our noise is to win games. Like today, the good feeling at the end of the game was just our fans and our noise." Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola lamented the red card decision. "Sixty minutes before the red card, players were very good. From then, City was obviously better than us," he said. "I didn't like the refereeing today. The first yellow card was nothing. It's a normal foul with 20 players behind the ball. As a referee you put yourself in trouble and us in trouble." The victory gave City six wins from six and moved them three points clear of Arsenal on 18 points, providing a forceful response on the pitch after a turbulent week away from it. Liverpool are ninth after their first league loss of the season. Maresca is only the fourth manager to win each of his first six Premier League matches with a club, after Pep Guardiola (City in 2016), Carlo Ancelotti (Chelsea, 2009) and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer (Manchester United, 2018-19). City's resounding victory comes with caveats. While they remain firmly in control at the top of the league, their perfect start increasingly stands in contrast to the uncertainty surrounding the club, with the fallout from the financial rules verdict leaving far more questions than answers about what comes next.

Source: Reuters

LIVERPOOL, England, Oct 11 : Premier League leaders Manchester City came to Liverpool's Anfield stadium on Sunday to find the fallout from their financial rules verdict waiting at the gates. It was their first game since being found guilty of 114 breaches of the league's financial rules, and Liverpool supporters had prepared a blunt welcome.  Fans drowned out the announcement of City's team with earsplitting boos and chants of "Going down, going down!" in reference to a possible relegation sanction. City deny the charges and are appealing.

In a raucous atmosphere among some 60,000 supporters at Anfield, one banner read: "A Generation Of Supporters Cheated" while some fans held three balloons making the number 114. Another two banners referenced Oasis songs, since the band's Liam and Noel Gallagher are devoted City fans. "All of your stars are fading away," read one, changing a line from the song "Stop Crying Your Heart Out," while another said "& after all, you really robbed us all," a parody of the song "Wonderwall." Liverpool fans are particularly angry as they were narrowly pipped to the Premier League title three times by Manchester City during the period in which they were deemed to have broken financial rules. "If they only get, say, a demotion to the Championship, and they can come back in one season, that's not enough. It should be more," said lifelong Liverpool fan David Matthias. "And as far as the titles they've won, I'd be quite happy to see them stripped of everything." BANANAS BACK Travelling City fans, meanwhile, held aloft inflatable bananas, a humorous tradition dating from their time out of the top flight in the 1980s. And they had the last laugh on the day, celebrating wildly after their team won 3-0 to subdue the Anfield faithful. "For every single fan, this is a lovely moment, which will stay with us for a long time," said goalscorer Erling Haaland. "It was tough and it was hard, but again we showed amazing character ... It's about these times to stay strong mentally, stick together, and do what you can do something about, and what we can do is to play good football and to fight together, because at the end, that's the only thing we can do." Outside Liverpool's ground, souvenir stalls did brisk business in flags and T-shirts bearing the word: "CHEATS." One flag depicted former City manager Pep Guardiola alongside players including Haaland dressed in black-and-red prison stripes, with "CHEATS" splashed across their backs and prisoner number 114.  It was gallows humour with a football twist, and a sign that the repercussions of the ruling had quickly spilled from hearing rooms into the tribal theatre of the Premier League. Merseyside police had been on high alert amid concerns City's team bus could be targeted after a social media post promoted a "Bus greeting." But while Liverpool supporters lining Anfield Road held aloft flares and sang anti-City songs, the team took an alternate quieter route to the stadium.  In 2018, City's team bus was struck by bottles, cans and flares before a Champions League match at Anfield and was damaged badly enough that a replacement was required for the journey back to Manchester.
